content: Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, {{v:6}} who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, {{v:7}} but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. {{v:8}} And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. {{v:9}} Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name, {{v:10}} that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth, {{v:11}} and that every tongue should confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

facets.text: Paul presents Christ's self-emptying as the pattern for the believer's own disposition, urging the Philippians to have the same mind that was in Christ Jesus. The great Christological hymn is not offered as abstract speculation but as the ground of Christian humility and self-giving love within the community. To think as Christ thought is to renounce grasping and to embrace lowliness for the sake of others.
facets.question: How does Christ's humility become the model for how Christians should treat one another?

facets.text: The hymn affirms that Christ existed 'in the form of God' and possessed equality with God, yet did not cling to it as something to be exploited. This declares the pre-existence and true divinity of the Son before his incarnation, a cornerstone of the Church's confession that Jesus is fully God. His refusal to grasp at what was already his own reveals the divine nature as self-giving rather than self-seeking.
facets.question: What does Scripture teach about Christ existing as God before he became man?

facets.text: Christ 'emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men'—the mystery the tradition names kenosis. He did not surrender his divinity but veiled its glory by truly assuming a complete human nature, becoming man without ceasing to be God. This self-emptying is the movement of the Incarnation, in which the eternal Son enters fully into the human condition.
facets.question: What does it mean that Christ emptied himself in becoming man?

facets.text: The descent reaches its depth in obedience unto death, 'yes, the death of the cross.' Christ's humility is not merely metaphysical condescension but a moral obedience that accepts the most shameful and painful death for humanity's redemption. The added emphasis on the cross underscores that our salvation is accomplished precisely through this obedient self-abasement, reversing the disobedience of Adam.
facets.question: Why does Paul emphasize that Christ was obedient even to death on a cross?

facets.text: The word 'Therefore' marks the turning point: because Christ humbled himself, God highly exalted him and bestowed the name above every name. Exaltation follows humiliation as its divine consequence, teaching that the path to glory passes through self-emptying obedience. This is the paschal pattern—the one who descends is the one who is raised up and glorified.
facets.question: Why is Christ's exaltation the result of his humiliation?

facets.text: That 'at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth' applies to Christ the worship Isaiah reserved for God alone (Isaiah 45:23). The confession that 'Jesus Christ is Lord' names him with the divine title Kyrios, revealing his universal cosmic sovereignty over all creation. His lordship draws the whole created order into adoration.
facets.question: What does it mean to confess that Jesus Christ is Lord over all creation?

facets.text: The hymn's final phrase directs all worship of the exalted Son 'to the glory of God the Father,' preserving the unity and order of the Trinity. The Son's exaltation does not compete with the Father's glory but consummates it, for the Father is glorified in the Lordship of the Son. Christian worship of Christ is thus ordered toward and fulfilled in the glorification of the Father.
facets.question: How does honoring Jesus as Lord glorify God the Father?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The Philippian hymn (2:5–11) presents Christ's pre-existent divinity, his kenotic self-emptying into human nature and obedient death on the cross, and his subsequent exaltation and universal Lordship, offered as both the pattern of Christian humility and the confession of Christ's true divinity to the Father's glory.

[MORAL | explicit]: Paul offers Christ's self-emptying humility as the model for how believers should think and treat one another in the community.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Christ existed in the form of God with equality with God, affirming the pre-existence and true divinity of the Son.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: The kenosis: Christ emptied himself by assuming a full human nature without ceasing to be God, the mystery of the Incarnation.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Christ's descent culminates in obedience unto death on the cross, accomplishing redemption and reversing Adam's disobedience.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The 'therefore' shows exaltation flowing from humiliation—the paschal pattern where the one who descends is glorified.
[SCRIPTURAL | traditional]: Every knee bowing and every tongue confessing Jesus as Lord applies Isaiah 45:23's divine worship to Christ, revealing his cosmic sovereignty and the divine title Kyrios.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: All worship of the exalted Son is directed to the glory of God the Father, preserving Trinitarian unity and order.
